fieldMarks: Largest rattlesnake, heavy-bodied, usually 1.0-1.5 m and sometimes over 2.4 m; males larger than females.
Olive, brown or near-black with diamond-shaped outlines of tan-yellow scales around blackish-brown centres down the back; keeled scales.
Large spade-shaped head, vertical pupils, pits between eye and nostril, and two light lines running from behind the eye to the back of the jaw.
Rattle at the tail tip; hatchlings (about 0.3 m) closely resemble adults.
behavior: Sit-and-wait ambush predator that coils in shade or underbrush; mostly diurnal but may be active at any time, with most activity early morning, evening and night per NatureServe.
Most activity April-October, though it visits the surface on warm winter days; hibernates singly; shelters in stump holes, burrows of gopher tortoises and other animals and brush piles.
Eats mainly rodents and rabbits (cottontails, marsh rabbits, cotton rats, squirrels); gives live birth in August-September to about 14 young.
habitat: Pine and wiregrass flatwoods, longleaf pine-turkey oak hills, scrub, coastal hammocks and barrier islands, dry prairie and abandoned fields, particularly with abundant cover; large tracts are most suitable; rarely climbs.
range: Southeastern coastal plain: NatureServe lists North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana; not recorded for Canada.
